I have an unabashed love of cooking games. This is not a cooking game - or if it is, it’s one that exists at the coalescence of Saw and Creature Kitchen - but that doesn’t mean I don’t love it anyway. Don’t Let It Starve is a horror/cooking-themed Balatro-like. You play as a chef trapped in a dungeon with a spooky and endlessly hungry creature. What specifically this creature is, you ideally never find out, but what you do know is that it craves bento boxes. Also human flesh, but mostly bento boxes. Gameplay centres on crafting bento boxes for our monstrous friend, filling them with tasty and correctly-shaped treats. Each round, players are presented with three ingredients for their bento boxes. While there is the option to reroll ingredients, the fundamental challenge is to make the best box possible out of the ingredients presented, with players potentially having the ability to manipulate the odds of certain ingredients appearing through power-ups and bonuses. Each ingredient that can be placed in the bento boxes is a different size and configuration, creating a multi-layered challenge. The game also includes a shop with bonuses and power-ups, with players being able to buy said tools using their limited funds. Players are both confronted with the microchallenge of fitting ingredients into their boxes, but also with the more familiar challenge of crafting a bonus set-up that scales quickly enough to keep up with the creature’s exponentially increasing demands. This is a game that activates both the Tetris-brain and the deck-building brain at the same time. I cannot understate how much I love this. I have played a lot of Balatro-likes, and while some execute on the formula in more innovative ways than others, I have yet to find one that is as unique as Don’t Let It Starve. The combination of mechanics, of both short and long term building, is phenomenal, and does wonders to make the game feel like a truly unique take on the genre. While the game can get repetitive within any given run - once you have a winning combination, there’s very little reason to switch away from it - this doesn’t detract from the fundamental satisfaction of putting things in boxes and watching numbers go brrrrr. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3743557302 Of course, Don’t Let It Starve falls into many of the same traps as other games in its genre. Runs live or die based on the initial few tools available in the shop, with the player’s ability to scale and what build they will be playing being determined fairly rigidly from the outset. If, for instance, I get a tool that gives bonuses every time I place a pickle in a bento box, you can rest assured that every box Monsieur Monstre will be getting for the rest of my tenure will be loaded with an unreasonable amount of vinegary goodness. This can make gameplay within an individual round start to feel repetitive. Once I have a formula that works, there is very little incentive to switch away from it, particularly given how short runs are. However, with runs only being 20-30 minutes, there is much more opportunity to explore possibilities through different runs. The game also tracks combos and bonuses across runs, allowing for a bit of a meta-progression. It’s one thing to have a bonus to pickles in one run. It’s even more satisfying to discover and know for all future runs that three pickles gives a large bonus, and I should therefore aspire to make every box nothing but pickles. Much like with Balatro, there are certain combinations that will always provide bonuses; unlike most Balatro-likes, these combinations have to be discovered through experimentation, making them all the more delicious when the player does discover one. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3743557472 The meta-progression extends beyond the immediate gameplay, however, and into the greater story as a whole. The bento chef, though trapped in their dungeon, is not chained to their bento table, and is instead free to wander the dungeon. It’s here that the game presents the player with puzzles and unlocks that carry over from run to run a la Blue Prince. Any particular run might be sacrificed in the name of advancing the mystery as a whole, and even a floundering run feels like it has promise because of the hope that one more reroll might reveal a new piece of the puzzle. The moments where I made forward progress on the game’s long-term puzzles felt genuinely satisfying and well-earned. While there is not some grand narrative to uncover here, there is nonetheless a satisfaction to be had from uncovering this dungeon’s small secrets. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3743557586 It’s within this combination of gameplay and narrative elements, of atmosphere and bizarre horror that Don’t Let It Starve really shines. Its gameplay is straightforward and fast-paced enough to be deliciously addictive, and its main antagonist is a joy to fear. There is enough of a mystery to make each run feel meaningful, while also providing enough variety for each run to be distinct. It is a fantastic little game that leaves its players with a very satisfying aftertaste. How this is different from Cloverpit: 1) instead of a slot machine, you arrange tetris pieces into a 3x3, 4x4, or 5x5 box. 2) You can reroll the tetris pieces. That's about it. Why? I cracked the safe and solved the sliding puzzle on my first and only run.

Playing this game honestly doesn't feel dissimilar to the one-and-only time I tried making a meal for my ex-situationship who just so happened to be a line cook. I felt like I was in a hostage situation. Food was thrown into the garbage out of spite. My plating was judged as if my life depended on it. And alcohol was the only thing that saved the dish, despite none of it going into the food. I might hit homeboy up again. 8/10: Really fun Balatro-like mixed with Tetris. Plus the game's Inscryption-inspired escape room vibes are -dare I say- ✨Delicious~✨

Really cool roguelike deckbuilder with many build options available, all wrapped around a satisfying Tetris-like mechanic of bento-making which is soo fun to interact with. I love the thrill of always trying to fill your entire bento and usually not making it, but when you pull it off those Balatro-like combo animations play and it feels soo worth it! Definitely recommend it for fans of the genre!

even though the game has multiple dificulties, it doesnt get more dificult, just more anoying and more restricting. olives are strong on 1 and 2 star dificulties, but in 3 and 4 star they are baisically requiered, as the dificulty modifires make all other foods unreliable and almost impossible to get a full bento(and non full ones reqire one specific tool to be close to usable) i had a lot of fun in the demo, but with the full game i just cant justify playing it for a long time. most runs you either horrible lack scaling for the score, or over shoot by a ton, there isnt really an inbetween. and a lot of legendary tools/chefs dishes are lacking, when they are supposed to be extreamly rare. if you are looking to kill a few hours, this is it, but anything more i cant see it.

This game is truly addicting and honest fun, the base game revolves around "Cloverpit" mechanics, but throws in its own satisfying gameplay loop. Along with tons of unique items to collect and Easter eggs to find, you can really sink loads of time into this. I'd give it a shot.

one of, it not the funnest roguelikes I've played so far!! I was never super into Balatro and other similar-ish games, but always loved the roguelike aspects like the deck building! Saw this game on passing when looking thru the summer sale, and played it a bit on stream. Everyone ADORED it, including me! I haven't had many games that have legit made me wanna binge it after first time playing and I can happily say this is one of the first, if not the best games to make me feel that way lol. I like the mix of silly and creepy aesthetics as well as the hidden room elements to figure out the bigger story, like Inscription! And the gameplay loop is addictive right off the bat with the instant item unlocks as you do better/get more combos! 12/10 game and would recommend to literally anyone and everyone, even strangers <3

"Clover Pit" type of the game but instead of slot machine, you place food in a bento in a puzzle-tetris style gameplay. It has secrets, unlocks and lots of different strategies to win the game so it has depth to keep you entertained and interested. For me, it has better progression and late game than other games of the genre that lose interest so early in the game. Great job!

A fun roguelike that captures the addicting strategy in same vein as clover pit and balatro. The game itself has a similar charm to it that feels inspired by clover pit or buckshot roulette in it's presentation while feeling distinct. The game is pretty light in the way of story telling but more than makes up for in the varity of touques and charms to make each round feel a bit different and fresh. If nothing else, if you're a fan of games that has you creating big scores or simply love the tonuge and cheek horror, I would definitely recommend giving it a try.
